doc.title: Virginia Mayhew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2022

chapter: Changes in the New York scene
title: 'Brooklyn white boy jazz'
summary: She explains her 1998 coinage for technique-heavy, bluesless modern jazz and why musicians moved to Brooklyn.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: would regret later and I probably will but I’m going to say it again now and I said there’s this thing happening — in 1998 — so that was a little over ten years after I moved there. I call it “Brooklyn White Boy” jazz. And it’s exactly what it has become, you know, the end of swing and blues and digging in and that would be — I know I’m a nasty person but that is the biggest change is like the standard when I moved here in ’87 was bebop was the standard. And now most of those people, now the people playing at the Village Vanguard are, I mean I would hesitate to say that to certain people but that’s really the school they’re in, they’re in this sort of Brooklyn white boy jazz school, which is now the main — to me it’s like it’s esoteric and it’s a lot of technique at all times and it doesn’t have any blues in it, and not to say that they’re not great musicians it’s just I don’t feel anything other than wow, that’s amazing that he can do that.
I think the key words you just said there was “at all times.” Lots of technique at all times.
But why Brooklyn? I don’t know, I don’t have a New York vibe. I don’t know too much about it.

Oh okay, already by the time I moved to New York most musicians had moved out to Brooklyn because of the rents. Not most, but many. And so that’s where the young musicians in particular lived, in Brooklyn. And so that was sort of where the scene was.
